chapter_theme: Old deeds (பழவினை) find their doer and settle each person's share of joy and suffering. Wishing, effort, holiness and learning cannot move that share, so the chapter ends by asking why anyone should grieve over it.
structure_note: The quatrains alternate between images from nature that no one made or can alter (the calf finding its mother, the round vilam fruit, rain that cannot be summoned or stopped, the palm and the millet seed) and the human cases they explain: decline, begging, wrongdoing by those who know better. Three quatrains (106 to 108) take apparent injustices and assign them to former deeds; 110 draws the conclusion that grief is pointless.

101.reading: A young calf let loose among many cows can still find its own mother, and an old deed has the same skill in seeking out the one who did it.
101.nuance: The image makes the deed active: it searches, as the calf does, rather than waiting to be met. Neither the verse nor Mudaliar says the deed comes from a former birth; Shanmuganar adds that.

102.reading: Beauty, youth, fine wealth and the awe one commands do not stay; one who sees this and still does not one good thing has a life that merely takes a body, stands, and falls.
102.nuance: The failure condemned is not vice but the absence of even one good act; the body is wasted rather than misused. Mudaliar offers two senses of ஒருவழி ஒன்றேயும்: any single good deed, or one deed of the kind that leads to the highest state.

103.reading: Everyone wants prosperity, but each person's enjoyments are measured out according to their own course, just as no one rounded the vilam fruit or blackened the kalam berry.
103.nuance: The fruits are chosen because their shape and colour belong to them by nature. The verse says only அவரவர் ஆற்றால்; both commentators take that 'way' to be one's former deeds.

104.reading: Not even the உறுவர் can remove what is bound to befall, and what is bound to be gained is the same; no one can bring rain in a drought or check it when it pours.

positions.position: The உறுவர் are sages, and destined pleasures can no more be prevented than destined pains.
No strong person can stop what fate brings, and no one can obtain by their own effort what they wish to gain.
positions.quote: பெற விரும்புகிறவற்றைத் தாமாகப் பெறுவதென்பதும் அதுபோன்றே இயலாததாம்

104.nuance: Mudaliar records Shanmuganar's kind of reading of the second line as another view, under which the verse is a reversed parallel: rain withheld matches gains withheld, rain unstoppable matches pains unstoppable.

105.reading: Men once as great as palm trees shrink to the size of a millet seed, hide their brightness within and live on diminished day after day; think about it, and what cause is there but the fruit of former deeds?
105.nuance: The verse turns a common sight, the fallen great, into an argument by elimination: no other cause can be thought of. Mudaliar specifies that the deeds are evil ones.

106.reading: If you ask why those who know the fruit of deep learning die while the unlearned live on, it is because the unlearned have none of the sap called sense, so Death passes them over as husks.
106.nuance: The verse is a joke with an edge: a long life for the unlearned is recast as Death's contempt. It doesn't say the learned die because of their learning; it supplies a fanciful cause, which Mudaliar names as a figure of imputed cause (ஏதுத் தற்குறிப்பேற்றவணி).

107.reading: When people with aching hearts stand at the gates of great houses, begging in sight of everyone, all of that is their former deeds, lord of the cool shore where swans tear the adambu flowers.
107.nuance: The address to the lord of the shore frames the quatrain as words spoken to a chieftain. Both commentators make the deeds evil ones from a former birth; the verse says only முன்னை வினை.

108.reading: When people who are far from ignorant, who know what ought to be known, still do blameworthy things, that comes from the deeds they have done, lord of the long cool shore where the breeze carries the honey-scent of the neythal.
108.nuance: The quatrain explains a moral puzzle, knowing the good and doing wrong, by pushing the cause back into earlier deeds. It explains the act; it does not excuse it, and pazhi still attaches.

109.reading: No one on this sea-girt earth wants evil in the least, and all want good results; but wanted or not, what is bound to come is hard to keep from touching them.
109.nuance: Desire is shown to be idle in both directions: wanting good does not bring it, and not wanting evil does not prevent it.

110.reading: What was set in the early mark does not shrink or grow, does not come out of order, gives no support in hard times, and arrives where it is due; so why grieve when the time of ruin comes?
110.nuance: சிறுகாலைப் பட்ட பொறி is literally 'the mark set in the small time'; both commentators read it as what was fixed in the womb. The chapter ends not with fear but with an argument for calm, since a fixed sum cannot be changed by grieving.

links.note: Both make a deed's consequence inseparable from its doer, with different images: the Kural's ruin stays at the heels like a shadow, and the Naladiyar's deed goes looking like a calf for its mother.
101 says the deed finds its doer among many; 120 says it is the only thing that goes with him at death. Together they make the deed both pursuer and sole companion.
Both draw the same conclusion from impermanent wealth: do the lasting good at once. 102 adds beauty, youth and standing to the list and condemns the life that does nothing.
Both say that enjoyment is measured out in advance: the Kural even for those who amass millions, the Naladiyar for all who want prosperity.

On Mudaliar's reading, 104 says that even sages cannot remove what is bound to befall. 269 says that those who attain the power of austerity can even leap past death. Both concern whether ascetic power can overcome what is coming; the tension holds if உறுவர் are ascetics and 269's கூற்றம் is fated death.

104 says no one can remove what is destined, as no one can make rain fall; 620 says those who strive without flagging see even fate's back. The tension depends on reading 620 as effort overcoming fate, as Pope and Kalaignar do.
Both describe the great brought low and give the same cause: in 3 the elephant-riders fall when their deeds are spent, and in 105 the palm-sized become millet-sized through former deeds.
Both deny that the unlearned truly live: the Kural says they can only be said to exist, like barren land, and the Naladiyar says Death will not even take them, as husks.

107 makes begging the outworking of the beggar's own former deeds, so the order that produces it is just. 1062 calls down ruin on whoever ordained that anyone should live by begging, treating it as an unjust order. The tension depends on 107's vinai being the beggar's own deeds.
Both describe one who knows and still does wrong. The Kural calls him the greatest fool; the Naladiyar traces the act to former deeds, which explains it without removing the blame.
Both say that a person's will has no say in what comes: in the Kural, care cannot keep what is not one's own; here, wishing cannot keep off what is due.
Both end a chapter on fate by asking why anyone grieves when the bad arrives, since it is as fixed as the good.

source_issues: 101: Shanmuganar's field ends with the Tamil text and Shanmuganar's commentary for 102, and 102 has no Shanmuganar commentary of its own.
Shanmuganar's verse numbers in this chapter run 31 to 40 rather than 101 to 110, and 110's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.
